title: Lateran IV, 1215
hook: the council uses the word transubstantiation and asks Catholics to confess and receive at least yearly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople, a city sacked by fellow Christians. Your line was sorrow, centuries later. Did an old apology come to mind? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

Where does the phrase Easter duty come from? Some Catholics still use it: the yearly confession and communion around Easter, the floor below which you don't go. It comes from a meeting of bishops in Rome, at the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral church. The same Pope Innocent from yesterday's story called it. Bishops and abbots came from across the West. They wrote decrees on all sorts of things, but two lines from that meeting are still part of ordinary Catholic life. Today's word is Lateran IV, the fourth council held there.
screen: `WHERE THE EASTER DUTY COMES FROM.` → `THE POPE'S CATHEDRAL.` → `TWO LINES THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: First line, about the altar. The council opens with a statement of faith, and in it, it says that in the Mass the bread and wine are transubstantiated by divine power into Christ's body and blood. That's the word transubstantiation, in a council's own text. The council didn't invent the belief. Catholics read it in Jesus' words in John's Gospel, which in the Douay-Rheims read: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." What the council did was give the belief a careful name: what the bread is changes, while what it looks like stays. Second line, about the heart. Another decree says that every one of the faithful, man or woman, once they reach the age of discretion, should confess their sins faithfully at least once a year to their own priest, and receive communion with reverence at least at Easter. Then, the surprise. Notice the words at least. This was never meant as the goal. It was a floor, a minimum for people who might otherwise drift for years. The council wasn't saying once a year is enough. It was saying, at the very least, don't go longer than this. Last, why it lasts. The Church still keeps both lines. Catholics call them precepts of the Church: confess serious sins at least once a year, and receive communion at least during the Easter season. Nothing stops a Catholic from going far more often. The floor is there for the years when life gets thin: at least once a year.
screen: `TRANSUBSTANTIATED: A CAREFUL NAME.` · `CONFESS AND RECEIVE, YEARLY.` · `A FLOOR, NOT A GOAL.` · `STILL A PRECEPT TODAY.` · then, large: `AT LEAST ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan your next confession, or, if confession isn't part of your life, plan your next honest look at yourself. Use the sit. First, think back: when was the last time? Don't judge the answer, just notice it. Then pick a real day and a place: a parish schedule you could check, a quiet evening you could set aside. Then let one or two things you'd want to bring rise to mind, without digging. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to keep the date. The bell holds the time.
Lateran IV. The fourth council at the Lateran in Rome, which named transubstantiation and set the yearly minimum for confession and Easter communion. Today's word.
Your line: at least once a year. Today, find one practice you've let slide below its floor, and put it back on a calendar. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes post regular times for confession, and the precepts of the Church ask Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year and receive communion at least during the Easter season; Catholics may go far more often.

Precepts of the Church per CCC 2042: confirm wording ('serious sins', 'during the Easter season').
